title: Value Matching: Scalable Reward-Guided Flow Adaptation
one_liner: Instead of burning memory retraining the whole model, learn one lightweight value function that tells the model which direction to steer generation to earn higher rewards.
lead: Large diffusion and flow models excel at generating images and molecules, but steering them toward specific rewards (like realistic images or stable molecules) requires retraining the entire billion-parameter model—a huge memory burden. This paper offers a smarter approach: learn one small auxiliary function that scores how good a partial generation is, then let the model use that score to decide which direction to nudge next, without touching the original weights.

problem.h2: The memory wall of steering giant models
paras: Diffusion and flow models work by gradual refinement: start with noise, and at each step add a bit more detail. To make the model generate images that satisfy some goal (like photorealism or toxicity) requires reward optimization—adjusting the step-by-step process to maximize the reward.

The naive approach: take the billion-parameter model, run it forward and backward computing how to adjust each weight to shrink the error. This demands enormous graphics-card memory, scaling directly with how complex the model is. For a 6-billion-parameter model, that's crushing overhead.

Existing shortcuts like Classifier Guidance sidestep the memory problem by learning a small auxiliary classifier offline and then using its scores to tweak generation. But this approach fails badly: the classifier was trained on a fixed dataset, so it struggles when the model tries to explore new regions it has never seen; and classifiers often cannot express complex, task-specific rewards.

callout.html: How do you steer a giant generative model toward high rewards without retraining it, and without being locked into what your training data showed?

steps.text: Initialize a random image or molecule.
Ask the value function to score the current partial image, because higher scores mean this state is on a path to high final reward.
Use the value score to bias the model's sampling toward high-reward directions.
At each generation step, ask the value function again—this explores regions the old training data never saw.
When trajectories finish, check their actual reward, then tell the value function whether its predictions were right, so it learns to recognize high-reward paths.

object.h2: The single thing the paper changes
paras: Instead of modifying the giant generative model itself, the paper adds a separate small neural network—the value function—that learns one thing: how good is each intermediate generation state (how likely is it to end up with high reward)? This value network becomes the steering wheel; the original model stays frozen.

hidden.name: The value estimate
paras: Value, in this context, is a single number that answers: given that we are partway through generating an image or molecule with a certain set of pixels or atoms, what is the expected reward we will earn if we finish optimally from here? It is not the final reward itself—that only comes at the end—but a prediction of what we will get.

The paper learns this by running generation trajectories (from noise to final output), measuring the actual reward at the end, and training a small network to predict that final reward from any intermediate state. As the model generates more examples, the value function updates by comparing its prediction to the real outcome, so on the next rollout it makes fewer errors and gets better at spotting which states point toward high reward.

heat.caption: Darker states have higher predicted value (more likely to finish with reward).

reads.html: Value is a guess: this half-finished image will earn high reward if we keep going smart.
The value function is learned via on-policy rollouts and trained to match the observed trajectory returns.

mechanism.h2: Why steering through a learned value function works
paras: Here is the core mechanism: you do not need to train the giant model to discover high-reward trajectories. Instead, train a small value function to recognize high-reward states. Once it is accurate, you can use it to bias the model's sampling at each step: when choosing which direction to nudge next, sample more often from actions the value function predicts will pay off.

Because the value function is learned on-policy (from whatever the model currently generates, including new regions the training data never covered), it adapts. If the model wanders into an unexplored but high-reward region, the next rollout will include that region, and the value function will learn to value it. This breaks free of Classifier Guidance's trap: you are not locked to the offline dataset.

The memory stays low because only the value function needs to be stored and updated. The original model is frozen; you only need memory for computing how to adjust the small auxiliary weights, not through billions of parameters.

Model generates next step with bias

math.h2: The equation: learning to predict the payoff
math.words: value_loss = (predicted_value - actual_return) squared, summed over all states in the trajectory
symbols: the value function's prediction at time step t
the partial generation state at step t
the actual cumulative reward earned from step t onward (observed after generation finished)

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Trajectory: start with noise, add details, end with final image.
Final reward measured: 8 out of 10 (realistic image).
At step 3 (halfway): value function predicted V(s_3) = 6, but later steps earned R_3 = 7. Error: (6-7)^2 = 1.
At step 7 (nearly done): predicted V(s_7) = 7.8, actual R_7 = 8. Error: (7.8-8)^2 = 0.04.
Update rule nudges the value function slightly so next time it predicts closer to 7 and 8.

math.note: The value function is tuned to predict what reward actually comes next, by comparing its guess to the real outcome on each trajectory.

charts.title: Classifier Guidance (offline, locked to training data)
charts.note: Small memory footprint but expressivity is limited and cannot adapt to new regions.

charts.title: Full fine-tuning (retrains whole model)
charts.note: Excellent performance but memory usage scales with the model size.

charts.title: Value Matching (learns small auxiliary, on-policy)
charts.note: Competitive reward performance, adapts to new regions, and uses only 5% of memory.

items.html: If the value function learns to overestimate the reward on certain types of states, the model will be steered toward chasing those false signals rather than genuine high-reward trajectories. Requires careful training and occasionally revisiting old data to calibrate.
If the reward you are optimizing (e.g., a toxicity classifier) is noisy or biased, the value function will learn to optimize the wrong thing. The model will faithfully chase poor signals.
If the value function becomes too confident too fast, the model may commit to one high-reward trajectory type and forget to explore others. On-policy learning can narrow the range of outputs.
Interleave exploration and exploitation, keep the value function calibrated against holdout data, and use a reward signal you trust.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Implement a small diffusion model (e.g., on CIFAR-10, a 32x32 image dataset) and a simple reward: score how close the generated image is to a target category (e.g., maximize dog-ness). Train the value function for 50 steps, using on-policy rollouts. Plot: (1) the mean reward over 10 generated images before and after value learning, (2) the value function's prediction error at each step (should shrink as it learns), and (3) the types of images the model generates—they should shift from random noise toward the target category.
demo.closing: The demo should show that the small value function, learned only from the model's own generation experience, reliably guides the model toward higher-reward outputs without storing billions of weight adjustments.
